This room is intended for discussion, implementation, and MSC drafting of Presence v2 via Selective Presence.

After https://matrix.to/#/!nD4Jy1hp0We0VmIM9ubjqWLBX_uV8YlTBBPa3a_v2uk/$pky9awpkMJUWeJPhTjcPaBZ7EPtAQ6rlKWUs9nCx66s, this room was created to promote discussion and help move forward the act of modernizing presence in the spec.

## Presence v2?

The following concepts for Presence v2 were discussed in that conversation, and I have given them the following names:
a. **Presence v1** (Push) - When a user goes online, an EDU is sent to every server that they share a room with, and these responses are sync'd to the users of those rooms. This is the current implementation, disabled on many homeservers. This introduces substantial write amplification: for 10000 servers and 50000 users, this is a worst case of 60k network requests (and often full TCP connections, barring HTTP2) sent. This isn't just on presence state changes: Synapse sends regular "heartbeat"-esque presence EDUs per online user to prevent them from triggering an offline timer.
b. **Socket Synced Presence** (Pull) - Servers keep long-lived persistent connections between each other to share presence data. Although this makes live data possible, it was rejected because it is very, very expensive and requires long-lived S2S connections, something intentionally not part of current Matrix.
c. **Polled Presence** (Pull) - Clients request specific users in view to them, and servers poll the origin homeservers regularly for presence changes. This is a feasible alternative to Selective Presence, and I would like to see investigation into this method as well, however this is out of scope for this room which specifically covers Selective Presence.
d. **Selective Presence** (Push) - Users opt-in for which other users they would like to see their presence data. Their homeserver pushes these changes to those specific servers - none more, none less. Inspired by Jabber/XMPP's current presence solution.

This room solely exists to discuss the Selective (push) Presence, as it is the best fit for the current Matrix federation model that I can see so far.

## Guiding Factors

* Opt-in presence solves many of the write amplification problems, while keeping presence usable for users who desire it.
* Presence should be incremental (see Cat's draft) and batched.
* "Rich" (live data) is technologically different from typical presence, though the line where they differ is unclear. Presence v2 may include rich presence, however that is out of scope for the first drafts. - Textual user statuses MAY be in scope, with this series of MSCs replacing [MSC4426](https://github.com/matrix-org/matrix-spec-proposals/pull/4426) if so.

## Prior Art

[Cat's draft "Incremental Heartbeat Assisted Presence," which these drafts build upon](https://github.com/FSG-Cat/matrix-spec-proposals/blob/FSG-Cat/Incremental-Heartbeat-Assisted-Presence/proposals/XXXX-incremental-heartbeat-assisted-presence.md)

[Federation EDU reconciliation](https://github.com/gamesguru/matrix-spec-proposals/blob/4e474f20c60b65e2da95cc4c9fbf7f74e6de8aac/proposals/0F02-federation-edu-reconciliation.md)

[XEP-0198: Stream Management](https://xmpp.org/extensions/xep-0198.html)

## Current Concept

Selective Presence allows users to select which users they'd like their presence changes to be pushed to. This is done through UI elements allowing users to select a list of "friends" (terminology may change later) likely to be stored within an account data event. Additionally, options such as room-wide defaults or DM based selection for who to trust by default. Their presence changes will be sent to those servers as an EDU listing which users they are to be sync'd to.

An extension to Simplified Sliding Sync will be used ("Sliding Presence Sync") and introduced in an MSC to allow clients to share with the server which users' "presence dots" are actively in view. This reduces overall write amplification of even selectively chosen presence - as the client is only receiving updates for clients actively in view. These two decisions together drastically reduce network requests sent for presence streams.

Additionally, to remove Synapse's unspecified presence heartbeat behavior, something similar to Cat's draft above will be implemented to allow presence states to realize if the users' server is online/offline. This will likely be its own MSC.

## Components

* MSCXXXX: Server-to-server heartbeats
* MSCXXXX: Sliding Presence Sync (depends on [MSC4186](https://github.com/matrix-org/matrix-spec-proposals/pull/4426))
* MSCXXXX: Presence v2 via Selective Presence

## Open Concerns

* Are S2S keepalives something useful to other areas of the spec? How might these actually look?
* What are the rules for when presence is sent to another user?
* Feedback from client/homeserver developers as to how this might actually look in reality
* Writing of drafts for all 3 MSCs
* How Rich Presence is related to these proposals (out of scope? handled by a similar mechanism in a future MSC?)
* If User Status Profile Fields are in scope for this MSC

m.new_content.formatted_body:
Current Concept

Selective Presence allows users to select which users they'd like their presence changes to be pushed to. This is done through UI elements allowing users to select a list of "friends" (terminology may change later) likely to be stored within an account data event. Additionally, options such as room-wide defaults or DM based selection for who to trust by default. Their presence changes will be sent to those servers as an EDU listing which users they are to be sync'd to.

An extension to Simplified Sliding Sync will be used ("Sliding Presence Sync") and introduced in an MSC to allow clients to share with the server which users' "presence dots" are actively in view. This reduces overall write amplification of even selectively chosen presence - as the client is only receiving updates for clients actively in view. These two decisions together drastically reduce network requests sent for presence streams.

Additionally, to remove Synapse's unspecified presence heartbeat behavior, something similar to Cat's draft above will be implemented to allow presence states to realize if the users' server is online/offline, so that presences can be permanent and the server going offline can be tracked. This will likely be its own MSC.

Components

  • MSCXXXX: Server-to-server heartbeats
  • MSCXXXX: Sliding Presence Sync (maybe depends on MSC4186?)
  • MSCXXXX: Presence v2 via Selective Presence

Open Concerns

  • Are S2S keepalives something useful to other areas of the spec? How might these actually look? maybe here?
  • What are the rules for when presence is sent to another user?
  • Feedback from client/homeserver developers as to how this might actually look in reality
  • Writing of drafts for all 3 MSCs
  • How Rich Presence is related to these proposals (out of scope? handled by a similar mechanism in a future MSC?)
  • If User Status Profile Fields are in scope for this MSC
  • Privacy components?

Hello everyone, just wanted to put my opinion out there of how this could work from the user's perspective:

> What are the rules for when presence is sent to another user?
I think there should be no sending to anyone by default, it should be entirely subscription-based.
Clients may give the option to subscribe to the presence state of everyone the user shares a DM with.
Additionally, the client could temporarily subscribe to the presence state of any user-profile the user is looking at (So when opening a profile, the presence state is fetched in the background and then displayed, maybe up to an hour. After that time, the subscription is dropped).

As a user, you would be able to turn off having your presence fetched by people you share a DM with.
You would also be able to turn off having your presence fetched by anyone you don't share a DM with, as a separate setting.

Having a state event in rooms to additionally share presence to everyone in there would be good for corporate environments, though users should additionally have an option to stop the homeserver from sending presence of them to these rooms.

I just realized, this would need a lot of keeping-track from the homeserver side, right? If a homeserver has 10k users, it needs to keep track of 10k people with different preferences of who can fetch their presence state.

the current gist of our proposal is:
- specific specification of batching behavior, especially for s2s EDUs and sync responses
- extension of presence TTLs to be far longer than Synapse's current ~30 seconds (a lot of the expensive part seems to be the "x is still online" not the state transitions)
- potentially using something like Cat's draft for Incremental Heartbeat Assisted Presence (as pinned) to use server "online indicators" (like recent receipt of a transaction, or the federation send backoff) to make presence potentially even _permanent_ until a server is seen as "down"
- potentially a sliding sync extension or something adjacent to prevent the write amplification caused by presence changes in large rooms (think about it - my server knows 10k destinations and 30-40k users...  in the worst case, that's 9999 EDUs sure, but also... 40k sync responses to people who don't even care about me!)
and then, of course, Selective Presence:
- an account_data event to list users and rooms to share presence EDUs with, alongside a room state event m.room.presence_sharing to act as a "default behavior" _hint_ for small rooms or DMs

The goal of using hints (cc [@kim:sosnowkadub.de](https://matrix.to/#/@kim:sosnowkadub.de)) is to provide that same behavior so that selective presence is not even noticeable to the average person who will be using presence in DMs or small rooms. If a user cares about privacy, they can change if they want to follow the hint, or disable sharing presence to the specific rooms they care about.

The algorithm would potentially get a little pricy though:

When a user's presence updates...
1. Start with an empty destination users set. 
2. If the user has "follow room presence hints" enabled:
  a. For every room that the user is joined to:
  b. If the room has the presence sharing hint enabled at its final resolved state, AND the room is not listed in the user's underride list:
  c. Collect the list of members in the room and add to the destination users set. 
3. For any room listed in the user's override list, repeat the above process. 
3. For any user listed in the user's underride list, remove the user from the destination users set.
4. For any user listed in the user's override list, add the user to the destination set.
5. Queue a "low-priority" EDU (not sure if a mechanism exists for this yet) to all listed server portions of the selected users containing this state transition. These EDUs can be sent to a specific destination user, because these low-priority EDUs are batched. The idea is a low priority EDU is to be sent on the next outgoing non-low-priority transaction to the target homeserver, or is force sent after some ttl expires.
6. Every $presence-ttl (>30 mins) repeat this process for every user with the online state.

When a server receives a presence EDU:
1. Store the state change of the user in memory or on short lived persistent storage
2. Queue a low priority sync response to all destination user's clients. This will not cause sync to return immediately and instead the EDU will be sent with the next sync response otherwise sent, or will be sent instead of the No Content response in a timeout case.
3. Clients are able to request the presence state of a user if it is available to them. This is only data from the local homeserver, though

My end goal with this is not to "add privacy to presence" - it's to fundamentally rebuild presence from the ground up. If we phrase it like that, and there's a measurable improvement **without impeding on the average user's use case** *and while providing OPTIONAL privacy features* (which this does), then you've successfully fixed presence.

## Our responses to MSC4325

1. There are two lists: allow and deny, permit and forbid, push and ignore, etc
2. These lists can contain multiple entity types: users, rooms, and servers
3. These lists of allowed and denied entities should be normalised at application time; that is, when the data event is received
   a) Servers cannot accept arbitrary amounts of redundant, incorrect, or meaningless data
   b) Therefore, they should reject entries that are both allowed and denied
   c) You could take this a step further and reject users or rooms that cannot be determined to exist, although I would be cautious
   d) Servers MUST ensure these lists are sanitised properly before sending them anywhere
4. The lists of allowed and denied entities must be subdivided per relevant homeserver, and only those lists sent to the homeservers in question

These decisions are designed to keep data transmitted over federation as light as possible. You may otherwise end up with EDUs that need to be broadcasted for hundreds or thousands of MXIDs, which is undesirable. In particular, keeping entity types at the S2S level affords easy granularity.

### Questions

* _What happens when the state of banned users in rooms diverges?_ (@stratself:muoi.me)
  * There seems to be no getting around this, you must contend with state divergence at either the sending or receiving server
  * The consequence of this is banned users potentially receiving presence they should no longer receive
  * Depending on which server resolves the lists to users, you can pick whether the sending or receiving server bears this load
* _How would DB queries remain performant here?_ (@gg:nutra.tk)
  * We anticipate that keeping indices (like _roomid_userid_) will help here
  * Measurements are required
* _How would the subdivision tradeoff between computation and federated JSON size actually measure?_ (@gg:nutra.tk)
  * We do not anticipate these operations will be compute intensive
  * Measurements are required
  * There is no real alternative, as sending your entire allow and deny listss to remote servers they are irrelevant to is a privacy leak
* _Should double-ended granularity be provided? That is, if a server is present in the deny list, but a user of that server is present in the allow list, should it be ignored, or should only that user of the server be allowed to receive the presence?_ (@lveneris:kludgecs.com)
  * Previously undiscussed

### Relationship with the other MSCs

These lists become the "override" and "underride" elements of the hints system. You could potentially only send _changes_ to these user setting lists to other servers, tying in with incremental behaviours, but in practice this might be a lot of work for not much good.

#### Further questions

One conclusion of the MSC4325 discussion was that it would be better for _receiving_ servers to resolve the "room" and "server" entity types to users, as they are better positioned to. Should they also resolve rooms with presence hints enabled? The sending server could collect rooms for which hints are enabled, and add those to the user's allowed entities list if the user has presence hints enabled. Alternatively, if you want to be more compute equitable, the sending server could resolve users for these rooms.

#### A revised algorithm

When a user's presence updates:

1.  Start with an empty destination set and exclusion set.
2.  If the user chooses to follow presence hints, then for every room the user is joined to,
    a. Check if the room has the presence sharing hint enabled in its state
    b. Check if the room does not match the user's deny list
    c. If a and b hold, add the room to the destination set
3.  Add all entries from the user's allow list to the destination set
4.  For each entry of the user's deny list, remove matching entries from the destination set and add the entry to the exclusion set
5.  Subivide the destination and exclusion sets into homeservers
6.  Queue a "low-priority" EDU for each listed server portion of the destination set containing this state transition and both relevant subdivisions of the destination and exclusion sets
    * These EDUs can be sent to a specific destination user, because these low-priority EDUs are batched. The idea is a low priority EDU is to be sent on the next outgoing non-low-priority transaction to the target homeserver, or is force sent after some TTL expires
7.  Every <PRESENCE TTL> (>30 mins) repeat this process for every user with the online state

When a server receives a presence EDU:

1. Store the state change of the user in memory or on short lived persistent storage
2. Resolve the accompanying destination and exclusion sets into the destination users on this server
3. Queue a low priority sync response to all destination users' clients. This will not cause sync to return immediately and instead the EDU will be sent with the next sync response otherwise sent, or will be sent instead of the No Content response in a timeout case
4. Clients are able to request the presence state of a user if it is available to them. This is only data from the local homeserver, though

In practice, I am not yet sure how the destination set should be kept light from the room resolution, because the system described above would only send the EDU to the server that "owns" the room. It may be reasonable to have the sending server figure out which servers are joined in the room, and add the room representation on those servers to the destination set to then have the local users resolved by those receiving servers. This is, in any case, less calculation than previously suggested, since the sending server does not need to do a full resolution, and the receiving server just calculates which of its own members are in that room.

  6. Queue a "low-priority" EDU for each listed server portion of the destination set containing this state transition and both relevant subdivisions of the destination and exclusion sets
    • These EDUs can be sent to a specific destination user, because these low-priority EDUs are batched. The idea is a low priority EDU is to be sent on the next outgoing non-low-priority transaction to the target homeserver, or is force sent after some TTL expires
  7. Every <PRESENCE TTL> (>30 mins) repeat this process for every user with the online state

When a server receives a presence EDU:

  1. Store the state change of the user in memory or on short lived persistent storage
  2. Resolve the accompanying destination and exclusion sets into the destination users on this server
  3. Queue a low priority sync response to all destination users' clients. This will not cause sync to return immediately and instead the EDU will be sent with the next sync response otherwise sent, or will be sent instead of the No Content response in a timeout case
  4. Clients are able to request the presence state of a user if it is available to them. This is only data from the local homeserver, though

In practice, I am not yet sure how the destination set should be kept light from the room resolution, because the system described above would only send the EDU to the server that "owns" the room. It may be reasonable to have the sending server figure out which servers are joined in the room, and add the room representation on those servers to the destination set to then have the local users resolved by those receiving servers. This is, in any case, less calculation than previously suggested, since the sending server does not need to do a full resolution, and the receiving server just calculates which of its own members are in that room (which it will certainly have a DB index for).

however:

* there is little tangible difference between asking a server to "send this to your users in these places" and to "send this to these of your users"
* you are equally reliant on the receiving server in either case, and it could choose to ignore your wishes regardless
* the receiving server knows more about its users than you do, and it will be able to resolve that information faster
* doing it this way divides up the resolution load into smaller chunks between each of the servers involved, instead of placing all of the load on the sending server. further to this point, imagine matrix.org having to do that resolution for the preference lists of _all_ of its users, and having to distribute those giant EDUs accordingly
* keeping the room and server entity types in the S2S object is more extensible down the road, for example it would enable the "per-room status" idea you mentioned

content.body:
ok so looking at the algorithm itself

* "destination" is ambiguous as it is commonly used to refer to _destination servers_, not rooms
* Checking if the room is ignored by the user should probably be done before checking the room state, as checking the room state is a more expensive operation than just filtering out rooms that we know we won't care about
  
  * The allow list should also probably be skipped when checking hints, assuming this means to always assume presence is allowed
* why is there an exclusion set at all? Isn't exclusion implied by a lack of exclusion in the destination set?
* "Subdivide the destination and exclusion sets into homeservers" what?
* defining "low priority" here will probably slow the proposal down as you then have to elaborate on what low priority even means. that'd probably best as a precursor proposal if anything
* heartbeat bad, don't do that
* You shouldn't suggest implementation details
* "Resolve the accompanying destination and exclusion sets into the destination users on this server" that's a LOT of information and a huge process to unpack, stuffed into a single line. That should be broken down.
* Again, "low priority" will only cause problems here. This will also require rather large changes on the server-side to how sync even works, so probably won't end up being implemented
* "Clients are able to request the presence state of a user if it is available to them" I assume this re-uses the existing API endpoints for this?
